Biology of Graft Incompatibility



Anatomy of compatible and incompatible tomato and pepper grafts


We’re investigating graft incompatibility in the Solanaceae, by comparing the anatomical and transcriptomic response between compatible and incompatible graft combinations.

Grafted tomato plants

title: Research: Plant Grafting
text:
Graft-induced Vigor



Lab member inspecting a grafted tomato plant in the greenhouse


Vegetable crop grafting onto interspecific hybrid rootstocks is used world-wide to increase abiotic and biotic stress tolerance and boost fruit production. We’re using genetics, transcriptomics, ionomics, and molecular and developmental characterization of vigorous tomato grafts to better understand the genetic basis of this phenomenon

Confocal images of a tomato/eggplant graft junction


We’re using heterograft genomics to characterize which RNAs and proteins move, understand how they move, and determine whether they have a function

title: Lab Members
text:
Current Lab Members







Dr. Margaret Frank


Principal Investigator



Margaret is a molecular plant biologist who is broadly interested in understanding how multicellular organisms communicate across tissues and organ systems, and applying this knowledge towards sustainable crop production. Margaret joined Cornell’s School of Integrative Plant Science (SIPS) in July 2018. Prior to moving to Cornell, Margaret was an NSF PGRP Postdoctoral Fellow at the Donald Danforth Plant Science Center in St Louis, MO, where she studied the dynamics of graft junction formation and graft-transmissible RNA movement.


Margaret earned her PhD at Cornell, working with Mike Scanlon on the evolution of shoot meristem patterning in early land plant lineages.


When she’s not doing science, Margaret loves to run, travel, and drink coffee.










Michelle Heeney


Ph.D. Candidate



Michelle is a PhD student in the Frank Lab and the Roeder Lab. She works on dissecting the underpinnings controlling and influencing long distance mRNA movement. Michelle graduated from the University of Massachusetts with two B.S.’ one in biology and one in math with a concentration in statistics. Her undergraduate thesis work focused on floral morphology in grasses, under the guidance of Dr. Madelaine Bartlett.


Michelle also worked in the biotech industry at the startup company Inari Agriculture where she developed her skills of plant transformation and bioinformatics.


Outside of the lab Michelle has a passion for film photography and fine art.










Zachary Joseph Ruwitch


Undergraduate Researcher



Zachary is an undergraduate researcher in the Frank Lab, working under the mentorship of Sam Yanders. He is majoring in Plant Sciences with a concentration in Integrative Genomics and Molecular Biology, and also conducts research in the Mazourek Lab at Cornell University. His academic interests center on plant genetics, molecular biology, and the role of agriculture in sustainable development.


Outside of the lab, Zach enjoys camping, canoeing, and rock climbing. He’s also a big St. Louis Cardinals and Blues fan.










Elise Boisvert


Ph.D. Candidate



Elise is a PhD student in the Frank lab where she works to shine light on the inner workings of grafted plants. She studies what is happening on a cellular and molecular level as the plant works to heal and join together. Elise started in the Frank lab during her undergraduate at Cornell. Her undergraduate work included a focus in rootstocks and root architecture, and in heterografting solanaceous plants to track mRNA movement.


Outside of the lab, Elise enjoys kayaking, hiking, and hanging out with her cute dogs.










Jessica Morgan


Post-Doctoral Researcher



More to come!










Tian Gong


Post-Doctoral Researcher



Tian is a post-doctoral researcher in the Frank lab. She’s working on grafted tomato production under high tunnel conditions.


Tian got her Ph.D. in Horticultural Sciences from the University of Florida.


Tian is known to enjoy exploring Ithaca and eating Cornell dairy ice cream in her free time!










Noor AlBader


Post-Doctoral Researcher



Noor broadly studies the transcriptional response to abiotic and biotic stressors in plants. Her work has encompassed staple crops such as rice, to novelty organisms such as chia and the beaver. Her genomic work has also led her to work on date palm and wild relatives of rice, with a focus on adaptation to desert and costal regions, respectively, at the Center of Desert Agriculture (KAUST).
She completed her PhD (2019) in the Molecular and Cellular Biology Program at Oregon State University (OSU). She is now a post-doctoral researcher, co-hosted by the Frank and Nelson labs.










Tin Aye


Undergraduate Researcher



coming soon!










Sam Yanders


Ph.D. Student



Sam is a PhD student in the Frank lab where she studies the mechanisms that regulate graft compatibility. She received her B.S. in Plant Sciences with emphases in Biology, Horticulture, and Crop Sciences from the University of Missouri. Her undergraduate research focused on the characterization of genes related to ATP stress signaling in the lab of Dr. Gary Stacey, as well as teaching undergraduate courses under the guidance of Dr. Mary Ann Gowdy.
In her free time, Sam enjoys kayaking, cooking, playing video games, spending time with friends, and making her dog wear funny clothes.










Israel Gabay


Post-Doctoral Researcher



Israel is a postdoc investigating the coupling of hydromechanical and electrophysiological processes in mediating long-distance signals in crops. His research aims to enhance our understanding of the inner communication system in plants and leverage this knowledge to guide crop improvement and plant bioengineering.
Israel holds a Ph.D. in mechanical engineering from the Technion - Israel Institute of Technology. He is hosted by the Frank and Stroock labs and supported by the Fulbright Fellowship.
In his free time, Israel enjoys spending time with friends and family and playing soccer.










Antone Jung


Undergraduate Researcher



Antone is mentored by graduate student Michelle Heeney and works jointly between the Frank lab and the lab of Dr. Adrienne Roeder.










Xing Ma


Laboratory Technician



Xing is a plant pathologist who pinpointed Dickeya dianthicola as the source of potato blackleg and soft rot outbreaks after 2014 in the Northeast US. His work also identified the potential of wild species Solanum microdontum to build better disease resistance into potato crops.
With a PhD from THE OSU and a decade of research experience at Cornell, Xing has deep expertise in pathogen genomics and bioinformatics. When he’s off the clock, you’ll likely find him researching computer parts for his next PC build, playing video games, or catching up on music.

Emma is an undergraduate researcher in the Frank Lab working under the mentorship of Israel Gabay. As a Chemical Engineering student, she is passionate about understanding how plants communicate and respond to their environment, with broader interests in sustainable agriculture and engineering approaches to biology. Outside the lab, Emma is a member of the Cornell Cheerleading Team and enjoys expressing her creativity through sewing, baking, and growing her collection of Smiskis. In her free time, she loves staying active through running and spending time outdoors.

Lucia just finished her freshman year at Cornell as a plant science major, hoping to minor in nutrition. Her academic interests include plant genetics, nutrition, food science, and community outreach/engagement.
Outside of the lab, she enjoys running, boxing, painting, and drawing, and engaging with the community.

Open Positions
The Frank lab is hiring enthusiastic and talented post-docs, graduate students, and undergrads. Prospective post-docs should send a CV, statement of research interests, and three references to Dr. Frank (mhf47@cornell.edu). Graduate students can apply through the Cornell Graduate School. Prospective undergrads can send Dr. Frank an email with their resume, a brief statement about their interests in plant science and molecular biology, and two references.

title: About Us
text:
Research in the Frank Lab
Scientific scholarship: We are advancing humankind’s knowledge of agriculture and science through cutting-edge research into plant signaling and development. Our work is built on exciting collaborations that extend across labs, institutions, and disciplines. We value open and transparent sharing of discoveries and tools. We adhere to a data management plan that ensures integrity, accuracy, and historic record keeping of our data. We acknowledge our sources and the resources that make our science possible. We support an environment that is open to scientists from all backgrounds.
Mentorship: We participate in growth-minded mentorship (Montgomery, 2019) to help shape the scientists of the future. A growth mindset is the belief that the talents and abilities of individuals can be developed or cultivated (Montgomery, 2019; Dweck, 2016). We believe in all lab members’ potential for success and strive for positive mentorship and learning opportunities for all lab members.
Outreach: We create and participate in outreach activities that expand beyond our academic communities so that the greater public can engage in our science and learn about how our work seeks to positively impact society.
Making our publications publicly available: We aim to post all of our original research manuscripts on BioRxiv prior to submitting them for peer review. When financially possible, we prioritize publishing in open-access journals to avoid the common “pay wall” and to make our research available to all.

Recent News

April 2025 - Samantha Yanders is awarded an NSF GRFP!

October 2024 - Elise Boisvert passed her A-exam and advanced to PhD candidacy.
August 2024 - Michelle and Margaret receive a FICUS award to collaborate with EMSL and JGI and identifying long-distance signals controlling biomass accumulation: https://www.emsl.pnnl.gov/news/thirteen-projects-funded-through-ficus-program
August 2024 - Former lab member, Hannah Thomas, starts her lab as a 100 Talents Young Professor at Zhejiang University. She also published the last chapter of her thesis in Hort Res: https://academic.oup.com/hr/article/11/12/uhae255/7755087

Etienne is featured here where he won one of the10 Global Challenge Awards at the Global Youth Institute in Des Moine, Iowa: https://www.instagram.com/p/DDNeYDdSpDP/?igsh=eGVyMGFjcjZpNDln
June 2024 - Margaret had her twins, Graham and Annabel 😱😱
May 2024 - Dr. Arielle Johnson and Dr. Nicole Szeluga defended their PhD theses. Arielle is now a postdoc in Jen Brophy’s lab at Stanford and Nicole is now a postdoc in Alex Harkess’ lab at Hudson Alpha.
Spring 2024 - Elise Boisvert and Kensy Rodriguez-Herrera AND Michelle Heeney Kenneth Buck receive Schmittau-Novak grants!
Spring 2024 - Our amazing lab tech, Sam Pelletier, picks the University of Minnesota’s Plant and Microbial Biology department for her PhD. She’ll be working in Katie Greenham’s lab!
Spring 2024 - Sam Yanders joined the Frank lab as a new PhD student!

Lots happened between February 2022 - Spring 2024, but Margaret was too busy to update the website.

Feb 2022 - Margaret is co-hosting the Northeast Regional Meeting of the Society for Developmental Biology (NESDB 2022) this spring
August 2021 - We welcome Audrey Widmier to the lab. She’ll be working on graft junction genetics as an NSF REPS intern!
August 2021 - Congratulations to Arielle Johnson for her recently published review in COPB titled: “Growing a Glue Factory: Open Questions in Laticifer Development”
January 2021- Congratulations to Yuanzheng Yue for publishing his doctoral and post-doc work titled: “Insight into the petunia Dof transcription factor family reveals a new regulator of male-sterility”
January 2021- Congratulations to Brandon Williams and Umair Ahsan for their recently published review titled: “Getting to the root of grafting-induced traits.”
October 2020- Allie Hermanson and Paul Chong, senior undergraduate research assistants, were awarded the American Society of Horticultural Science’s Scholarship Achievement Award.
October 2020- The Frank lab is happy to welcome Hamid Razifard as a new post-doctoral researcher. He joined the lab from UMAmherst where he studied the evolution of Solanum.
August 2020: Collaborative publication with Xia lab is printed in Science Direct: “TBtools: An Integrative Toolkit Developed for Interactive Analyses of Big Biological Data”. doi.org/10.1016/j.molp.2020.06.009
July 2020: The National Science Foundation recently awarded Frank a five-year, $1.3 million Faculty Early Career Development Program grant for her proposal, “Harnessing the Plant Mobileome to Predict, Design, and Deliver Long-Distance RNAs in Plants.” See article.
June 2020: Hannah Thomas awarded USDA Pre-doctoral Fellowship for “Understanding the role of intercellular communication in vegetable crop grafting” See article.
May 2020: Frank Lab takes part in collaboration with Ithaca Children’s Garden (ICG), to create 1,000 at-home gardening kits for local families. See article.
